preview: An account of the 2020 virtual recruitment process for a Wells Fargo summer internship, detailing the AMCAT online test, technical interview, senior manager round, and HR interview.
content: Wells Fargo Summer Internship Interview Experience 2020 Akshat Shah Information Technology 2018-2022 The year was 2020 (screams), so the entire process was held virtually. There was an online test on Aspiring Minds (AMCAT) and three rounds of interviews were held the next day. Even for the online test, there were some eligibility criteria. In this instance, only CS and IT students were eligible, and there was a CPI criterion of 8 (I’m not sure about this). There were about 70 students who gave the online test. 0. Pre-placement talk: Seriously, pay attention. It can help you get information that will help you to converse with interviewers, and it would probably be a good idea to know the company you want to do an internship at. 1. Online Test: On AMCAT, webcam-proctored a. English Section: This tested basic English Language skills. All questions were single-answer MCQs. There were around 14 questions and 15 minutes to solve them. They were of the following types: i. Fill in the blank by selecting the word which is most suitable for the given sentence ii. Improve sentence construction iii. There were 2-3 passages, and there were 2-3 questions based on each. These tested comprehension skills, whether one has understood the meaning of the passage. The last few were slightly tricky. This section was very easy. b. Data Interpretation Questions: This section had 13 questions and 25 minutes to solve them. Some of them involved a scenario of an industry; background information and some tables were given. Based on these, there were some logical business questions. For example, a firm is paying more to its employees than other firms, should it decide to lower the pay of its employees? On the other hand there was information from a study that lower pay results in lesser quality and hence lesser sales. You didn’t need to know business to solve these, just logic. 3-4 questions were based on a box-plot of stock prices for some days, and it had some tricky and mathematical questions. These weren’t very direct, and ate up a lot of my time. 3-4 questions were based on airline ticket prices. Data of different discount schemes available, and different criteria for availing those schemes was given in checked tabular format. For example if C1, C2, … are the criteria, and S1, S2, … are the schemes, if C1 and C3 are satisfied, then S5 can be availed. And the questions were like a family had to book tickets, and each of the members had different characteristics (like frequent flyer, infant), so find the total cost. I took too long to solve the stock and airline problems, so I couldn’t solve the last 4 questions, which were based on some other scenario. So I just marked them randomly. (There was no negative marking. Other tests may have it, so always know this before giving every test.) c. Coding Questions: I must say that I got lucky (and I’ll probably keep saying this throughout this document). Everyone had 2 coding questions to solve in 60 minutes. The questions that I got (yes, problems weren’t the same for everyone) were really easy. i. Count the number of occurrences of a string in another substring. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/frequency-substring-string/ Although there is an O(M+N) solution, my O(MN) solution was accepted, since string length was a maximum of 15 (naive matching). ii. The second problem was similar to the reachability to the end of an array question. It was coated in a long problem statement about a network which has nodes linearly connected, and one can install a repeater at that node so that signals can go further down the array of nodes. Every node has a certain value that represents how many nodes ahead can the signal go if a repeater is installed there. So the problem was to find the sequence (ordered) of nodes at which repeaters should be installed, such that a signal from the first node can reach the last node, and minimum repeaters have to be installed. If there are multiple solutions with a minimum number of repeaters, print the one which is lexicographically smallest. Constraint: N <= 10^3, so I solved this using dynamic programming 22 people were shortlisted for the first round of interviews, the Technical Round. Interviews were taken on Zoom calls 2. Technical Interview: 45 minutes The interviewer started with asking me to introduce myself. Then he asked me about the subjects that I had in my current semester (V). Then he started with the questions. a. OS: Semaphores, difference between threads and processes, paging, cache. b. OOP: Principles (abstraction, encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance). c. COA (-_-): Pipelining. I didn’t remember the term. d. CN: TCP/IP stack. He then asked me about routing algorithms. I didn’t know that, so I told him that we haven’t covered that yet (I had told him that we had CN in the current semester). He said okay and continued. e. DBMS: He asked me about Normalization, and B+ Trees. I did not know B+ Trees (-_-) f. He asked me about the first project that I had mentioned on my resume. He did not ask any technological aspects of it, just what the project was. g. Since two of my projects used JavaScript, he asked me about OOP in JS. I answered this very haphazardly. h. DSA: He asked me two problems. He asked me whether I wanted to write it on paper and share photographs to him or whether I wanted to use some collaborative editor. I opted for the latter. So he sent me a collabedit link. There was no syntax highlighting, no bracket completion, no auto indentation, so always make sure to write clean and readable code, regardless of the editor. He asked me for the pseudocode, in plaintext, but I ended up writing both questions in C++ :-P : i. Longest increasing subsequence with reconstruction: This is a standard DP problem, with O(N^2) complexity. I solved it and explained each part to him. He asked me to analyze the time and space complexity. Then I told him that an O(nlogn) solution also exists for LIS, but I didn’t know how it worked. He didn’t ask me any questions on this further. ii. Reverse a 32 bit unsigned integer: I thought this was easy, so I just solved it using shifting bits and checking if each bit was 1 or 0. And the interviewer also accepted this solution. After the next round of interviews, my friend made me realize that my solution is not correct. For example, if the number given is 6, or in binary: 0000...0110, the output should be 0110….0000. But my solution would give the answer as 0000...0011, or 3 in decimal. :-) Despite my blunder for the second DSA question, I qualified for the next interview round, along with 14 other people. 3. Senior Manager Interview: As you can guess, the interviewer was someone at a senior position. This interview lasted for 1 hour. a. He asked me to differentiate between Java and C++, garbage collection in Java (because I mentioned this difference) - when exactly is the garbage collector called, and whether setting a class variable to null causes the garbage collector to be called immediately, abstract classes v/s interfaces. He was listening very intently, and he somehow always picked something that I had said in response to the previous question, and then asked a counter question. b. He asked me some DBMS questions, like what are primary keys, can unique keys be NULL and an example based question. He asked me to write a query to select duplicate rows. I told him a query, he said I was close, and went on to asking me questions about GROUP BY. c. He asked me nothing from OS or DSA. d. He asked me exhaustively about my projects, my role in them and some DOM questions because I’d used JS. He patiently and intently listened about my projects, and asked specific questions related to them. e. He asked me about challenges and my roles at SRA and CoC (I had mentioned these on my resume). f. Then he asked me if I had any questions for him, so I asked one. In the middle of answering it, he actually asked me the following question (it was open-ended). I asked for clarifications twice, and I’m still not clear about what he was asking me: Say you’ve been given the task to make an application that takes real time stock prices from a database and relays these prices to some interface (web / API client / whatever), and you’re told to make this application in Golang and in Java. How would you approach this task, and how would you present your application (he stressed on the word “metrics”)? So I think that he wanted to know how I would plan the project activities, and deal with having to code in an entirely new language for me (he knew beforehand that I didn’t know Golang). I mentioned a few points like learning Golang first, and simultaneously designing the application, the inputs, outputs, architecture (I was just saying whatever came to my mind at that point). Then I would implement it in the two languages. Then he asked me about metrics, so I mentioned speed, scalability, code quality. For some reason I also blurted out “Design Patterns” when I was talking about code quality. So he asked me what Design Patterns are, and what the Singleton Pattern is. (That is the one design pattern I was confident about at that time XD). After a long wait (like, 8 hours for me) 8 people made it to the last round, HR. 4. HR Interview: This was just for 15 minutes, and it was really quick XD. The interviewer asked me what I know about Wells Fargo and why I wanted to intern there (pay attention during the pre-placement talk :-) ). He then asked me which companies I had given interviews for before and what I had learned from those interviews. He then asked me if I’m flexible with the locations of the internship. And finally, he asked me if I had any questions for him. All 8 people who qualified for the HR round were selected for the internship. Afterword (or whatever it’s called): 1. I know this document is long, but I wanted to include how interviewers can ask counter questions, how they can be very thorough with your resume, et cetera. 2. If you’ve been preparing well, then don’t get demotivated if you don’t advance to next rounds. There were days when I had become very demotivated due to not even qualifying the online rounds. I had failed learning experiences with a total of 6 companies before being selected for this internship. Learn from your mistakes. 3. One internship drive does not define you or your worth. Stay confident, persistent and enjoy what you’re learning. 4. Plan. I had all my focus on DSA, and I ended up doing OS, DBMS haphazardly. 5. If you’re a person who doesn’t speak too much, try developing a habit of speaking out loud when you’re solving a coding problem. In an interview, it’s much more important to explain to the interviewer your thought process and then arriving at a solution. Maybe it’s not perfect, but it’s better than thinking silently for two long, awkward minutes. 6. People will keep giving you tips (like I am right now :-P), and you should listen to them. But remember that your hard work and your calmness during the interview are the things that will help you the most. If you have any queries, you can email me at akshatshah_21@yahoo.in All the best for your endeavours!
